To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

species variation in leaf and litter calcium concentration is linked to soil Ca supply, but that the variation in leaf calcium among species cannot be explained by variation in root distribution in the soil profile.

(1) there was a four-fold difference in leaf-litter calcium concentration among 14 temperate tree species growing in central Poland, (2) this variation was not explained by differences in root distribution in the soil, (3) species differences in leaf Ca were linked to variation in forest floor turnover rates and earthworm abundance, and (4) variation among species in leaf calcium concentrations of greenhouse-grown seedlings was positively related to variation in leaf Ca of mature trees in the field, and
“Species differences in leaf and litter calcium among 30-year-old temperate tree species were due to both soil and species differences in calcium uptake and growth response to low calcium.”.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role that Ca plays in the growth, development, and physiology of trees and how this role may be related to Ca concentrations in leaf tissue.
understanding the mechanisms that control variation in leaf and leaf litter calcium concentration among tree species.

the hypothesis that differences in leaf Ca among tree species are due to differences in root uptake, growth, and partitioning of Ca to different organs, and that these differences are related to the distribution of tree species in forest communities and the cycling of Ca in ecosystems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Ca concentration in the green leaves and the litter of the trees is a function of the Ca uptake, the growth of the trees, the Ca translocation to other organs, the soil Ca supply, and the soil pH.
the species differences in leaf litter Ca are due to a complex interplay of soil properties and physiological differences among species.
the variation in leaf and litter calcium is a result of the interaction of several environmental and biological factors, and that the relative importance of these factors varies among tree species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
leaf and litter Ca are not simply a function of Ca supply, but are also controlled by the physiological capacity of trees to acquire and retain Ca.

the variation in Ca concentrations of green leaves and litter among tree species in the field is due to both differences in Ca uptake from the soil, and differences in the translocation of Ca to different plant organs, with the latter being the more important of these two factors.

leaf Ca concentration of mature trees is a function of species, with the species differences being maintained under a variety of Ca regimes, including those of the common garden in which we grew trees, and those of the greenhouse.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the same ranking of species in leaf Ca concentrations exists both in the field and in the laboratory, indicating that this ranking is a stable species trait.

species differences in leaf Ca concentration are due to a combination of soil factors and physiological differences among species, and that species differences are not simply due to differences in uptake or growth.
leaf and litter Ca concentrations of trees are not necessarily good predictors of soil Ca availability.
